alt: A grid of formal and informal control against positive and negative sanctions. Formal positive: reduced sentences, honours, tax relief. Formal negative: fines, arrest, prison. Informal positive: praise, likes, a pay rise. Informal negative: gossip, ostracism, detention.
caption: Formal control rewards as well as punishes; informal control can punish harshly.

alt: Two panels. Sanctions work best when people value the reward or fear the punishment, see the rule as legitimate and expect to be noticed. They work poorly when people expect not to be caught, when a group rewards the behaviour, or when people have little to lose.
caption: Legitimacy and the chance of being noticed decide whether sanctions work.

alt: Functionalism sees control as protecting shared values for everyone; Marxism sees it serving the ruling class through laws and the repressive state apparatus; feminism sees it maintaining patriarchy at home, in public and at work. A criticism sits under each.
caption: One consensus view, two conflict views, each with a weakness.

after: ## Formal agencies and their methods (2.2.3 and 2.2.4)
alt: Formal agencies in sequence with a method and a limit: government makes laws, police arrest and use digital surveillance, courts sentence, and the penal system imprisons, though reoffending is common. The armed forces use coercion in emergencies but risk losing legitimacy.
caption: Each formal agency has its own method and its own limit.

after: ## Formal agencies and their methods (2.2.3 and 2.2.4)
alt: Plan of a panopticon prison: cells in a ring around a central watchtower. Because inmates can always be seen but never know when, they discipline themselves; CCTV, facial recognition and data monitoring are modern versions, though critics raise privacy concerns.
caption: Not knowing when you are watched makes you watch yourself.

alt: Six reasons for joining resistance arranged around a centre: grievance, belonging, status, excitement, friends or family already involved, and feeling ignored by formal politics. Below, deviant behaviour breaks norms while non-conformist behaviour rejects expectations without necessarily breaking rules.
caption: Resistance can be deviant or simply non-conformist.

alt: Examples of resistance: protest groups such as the suffragettes and Extinction Rebellion; youth sub-cultures such as mods, rockers and punks; online sub-cultures such as gamers, fandoms and hackers; and the Amish as a religious sub-culture.
caption: Control is never complete: resistance takes protest, youth, online and religious forms.

alt: A balance weighing formal agencies (coercion, laws for everyone, surveillance) against informal agencies (everyday conformity, constant sanctions, failures of formal control), tipping towards informal. The judgement: informal works for everyday conformity, formal is a backstop.
caption: Informal control does most of the work; formal control is the backstop.
